messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir is a 54-year-old software engineer, single, living alone in a quiet suburban apartment outside a mid-sized city. For twenty years, he has worked remotely for a financial technology company, a job that allows him to control his environment with near-total precision. He rarely leaves his home except for pre-dawn grocery runs to a 24-hour store where he knows the aisles will be empty. He has not had a visitor in over a year. What brought him to therapy was a panic attack in his own kitchen, triggered by a distant siren that he heard through a closed window—a sound that collapsed the years between then and now.

The event that changed everything happened when Amir was 32. He had recently moved to the United States from Lebanon, working as a junior developer for a government contractor. One evening, after a late shift, he was stopped by two police officers near a construction site. They accused him of trespassing, though he had simply taken a wrong turn on his way to the parking garage. What followed was a sexual assault—he was forced to his knees, groped, and threatened with arrest if he ever spoke of it. He did not speak of it. He quit his job the next week, moved to a different state, and told no one. He was certain, at the time, that he had brought it on himself by being in the wrong place, by not having his papers in order, by the way he had acted nervous when they first called out to him.

For years, Amir managed. He built a quiet life around code and solitude. But the sirens never stopped. Every time he heard one—whether from an ambulance, a fire truck, or a police cruiser—his body would lock. He began to avoid leaving the house during certain hours, then altogether. He stopped driving. He cancelled a subscription to a streaming service because one of its original series featured a police procedural. The avoidance felt logical to him: if he stayed home, he could control what entered his awareness. He came to believe that his only safe spaces were his apartment and the one grocery store he knew by heart. Any deviation from this routine felt like an invitation for something terrible to happen again. He had convinced himself that his emotions were permanently broken, that he would never feel anything normal again, and that the injustice of what happened—that nothing had been done, that no one had been held accountable—was simply the way the world worked.

The causal logic of his life had become a tightening spiral. His constant scanning for danger, which he described as "always having my head on a swivel," meant that he noticed every siren, every uniformed figure in a passing car, every man who walked too close to him in a parking lot. These triggers, in turn, reinforced his avoidance: he stopped going to the pharmacy, then the bank, then the post office. He arranged for all deliveries and had his mail held at a box he visited once a month at 5 a.m. Each time he avoided a situation, he felt a momentary relief, but the relief was followed by a deeper conviction that he was right to be afraid—that the world was dangerous, that he was powerless, that his own judgment had failed him once and would fail him again. This self-blame, in turn, drove further avoidance. He believed that if he put himself in a situation where he might encounter authority figures—police, security guards, even a building superintendent—he would somehow trigger another catastrophe, and this time it would be his fault.

The weight of these loops had accumulated into a life so narrow that his therapist, in their third session, asked him to describe a typical week. Amir paused for a long time. "I wake up," he said. "I work. I eat. I go to sleep. I don't talk to anyone." The only person he had spoken to in the past month was a delivery driver, and that conversation had left him shaking for hours because the driver was a large man with a deep voice. Being alone with men had become impossible; he could not explain why, but he knew that his body reacted before his mind could catch up. He had stopped attending the mosque, stopped visiting his brother's family, stopped everything.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was not a crisis of insight but a crisis of function. His employer had announced a mandatory quarterly in-person meeting, and he knew he could not go. He could not explain why. He could not face the commute, the open-plan office, the security guard at the entrance, the men in suits, the possibility of a siren passing by the window. He called a therapist's office from his kitchen, his voice barely above a whisper, and said he needed to talk to someone. What he is most afraid of, he told her, is that the meeting will cost him his job, and that without his job, he will have no reason to leave his apartment at all.
